Occasional findings of skeletons permeated by small to

multiple osteolytic foci with perforated skulls may create diagnostic problems. Firstly, in vivo processes should be distinguished from postmortem changes. Among external factors, several species of insects, especially beetles, devour wood and bone in order to put their larvae into the holes. $^{1,2}$ Such a case can be demonstrated from the Christian site of Sayala (Egyptian Nubia, sixth to eleventh century AD). The skull of a 40-50-year-old male (J1/6) showed, macroscopically, a row of five greater (4-5 mm diam.) and three smaller (1 mm diam.) holes along the longitudinal axis of the left parietal bone. Other small openings were scattered near the lower edge of the same bone and in the left temporal. Still more of them could be detected on the inner surface of these bones. On the radiographs their quite similar size, round and in places elongated form can be observed (Figure 1). Dr. Schulz from Göttingen examined these clearly bored-out channels histologically. In electron microscopic pictures he even detected remnants of the covers of wings of adult beetles as well as arm and leg fragments from their larvae (M. Schulz, pers. comm.). Only the above-mentioned region was affected. Other parts of the skull and the postcranial skeleton were devoid of any changes.

If we exclude such pseudopathologies, we have to consider in vivo causes of multiple osteolytic lesions, especially the most commonly occurring disorders — myeloma multiplex (MM) and lytic metastatic carcinoma (LMC). Both are not the result of new growth of bone cells, but of malignantly degenerated cells of different origin. In MM (plasmocytoma, myelomatosis, morbus Kahleri) these are the plasma cells of the blood-forming bone marrow. Each focus of the disorder arises as an independent development in a systematized disease. $^{3}$ Most authors who take into account the place of origin and the clinical course of the disease, place it in the group of primary bone malignancies. Only Ortner and Putschar $^{4}$ preferred to classify it under the heading of reticuloendothelial and haemopoietic disorders together with lipid storage disorders, histiocytosis X, anaemias and leukemia.

Today, at least 76 per cent of tumours with metastases coming to autopsy involve the skeleton. $^{4}$ Therefore, in the absence of radical surgery of the primary foci in the past, a high frequency of skeletal metastases could be expected. However, because of the lack of any treatment in the past, many patients may have succumbed at an earlier stage of the cancerous disease, especially if it afflicted important internal organs, such as a lung, kidney or the stomach. $^{3}$

To understand the landscape of skeletal metastases, we must first look at the modern data, which serves as a baseline for interpreting historical remains. When cancer spreads (metastasizes) to the bone, it does not do so randomly; it has a strong preference for specific primary tumor sites.

Of the different locations of primary carcinoma, osseous metastases recently have been most common in breast (47.2 per cent), prostatic (42.4 per cent), thyroid (30.8 per cent) and lung carcinoma (29.8 per cent), $^{5}$ as well as in stomach and kidney carcinoma. $^{3}$

of bone destruction is just as critical as the location. This is where the concept of **osteoplastic** versus **lytic** metastases becomes essential.

This distinction is vital for paleopathologists and radiologists alike. If you see dense, white patches on a bone scan, you think prostate. If you see "punched-out" holes, you think lung, kidney, or breast.
In the last 15 years several authors have discussed the question of the differential diagnosis between MM
LMC (Leukemic/Metastatic Carcinoma, often referred to here as metastatic carcinoma). This is a notoriously difficult task because both conditions can present with similar patterns of bone loss.
For Grmek the differential diagnosis 'est souvent très difficile, voire impossible'
(is often very difficult, if not impossible)
except 'en cas de carcinomas secondaires de nature mixte où l'ostéophytose côtoie les foyers
d'ostéolyse' (in cases of secondary carcinomas of a mixed nature where bone growth sits alongside foci of bone loss).
At the same time, however, he was already aware that 'l'abondance et la dispersion des foyers d'ostéolyse favorisent le
myélome' (the abundance and dispersion of foci of bone loss favor myeloma).

Let’s unpack Grmek’s insight. He is suggesting that while the two diseases look similar, the *pattern* of the holes matters. In Multiple Myeloma, the bone loss tends to be widespread and numerous. In contrast, metastatic carcinoma might show a mix of bone building and bone breaking.

In spite of the fact that Steinbock $^{6}$ described both lesions under separate headings, he pointed out that 'multiple lesions (of LMC) often closely resemble the punched-out lesions of MM' and that a 'differential diagnosis between metastatic carcinoma and MM is difficult'. $^{6}$ At the same time he quoted Jacobson, who observed that the vertebral pedicles were more often involved in LMC than in MM (94 per cent versus 15 per cent) and who pointed out that the foci of MM appear more constant in size and more numerous than those of MC. $^{8}$

Here, Jacobson provides two crucial diagnostic clues that act as a "fingerprint" for each disease:
1.  **Location Specificity:** The **vertebral pedicles** are the bony arches that connect the front of the spine to the back. Jacobson found that metastatic carcinoma (LMC) loves to attack these specific structures (94% involvement), whereas Multiple Myeloma rarely does (only 15%). If you see damage to the pedicles, it is a strong indicator of metastatic cancer.
2.  **Lesion Morphology:** The "foci" (the individual spots of disease) in Multiple Myeloma tend to be **more constant in size** and **more numerous**. Think of it like a spray of uniform paint droplets. In contrast, metastatic carcinoma lesions can be more variable in size and number.

Neither are Ortner and Putschar more optimistic, because 'in the skeleton these two types of cancer reflect a morphological gradient making differential diagnosis impossible in many cases'. $^{4}$ As a means of differentiating 'between disseminated MM and LMC, particularly of the breast'... 'the male prevalence in myeloma and the female prevalence in breast cancer are helpful'. $^{4}$

Ortner and Putschar acknowledge the "morphological gradient"—meaning the visual differences are often subtle and overlapping, making a definitive diagnosis from bone alone nearly impossible in many cases. However, they offer a pragmatic solution: **epidemiological context**. Since Multiple Myeloma is statistically more common in men, and breast cancer (a major source of LMC) is overwhelmingly female, the sex of the individual becomes a powerful diagnostic tool. If you have a female skeleton with widespread lytic lesions, breast cancer is a leading candidate. If you have a male, Multiple Myeloma rises in probability.

In spite of the fact that in his first contribution to this problem Suzuki $^{9}$ agreed with the difficulty of differential diagnosis between MM and LMC, which quite often create similar conditions in dry bones, he pointed out that diffuse clear round lytic lesions are typical for MM, while relatively large and restricted defects are more common in LMC. According to this and the punched out character of the lesions without any bone sclerosis in a skull of the Edo period in Japan, he diagnosed MM. In contrast with this, Suzuki $^{10}$ found a skeleton from Kitami, Hokkaido, with osteolytic lesions in the skull, spine, ribs, scapulae and pelvis. He observed that 'in the parietal region, numerous concentrated small lytic defects ... seem to form a comparatively large osteolytic lesion as a whole'. In radiographs this lesion 'revealed an obscure and relatively large osteolytic shadow'. Both features led him to a diagnosis of LMC.

Suzuki’s work illustrates the application of these rules in real-world paleopathology. He identified two distinct patterns:
*   **Multiple Myeloma (MM):** Characterized by **diffuse, clear, round lytic lesions**. In his case study of an Edo-period skull, the lesions were "punched out" and lacked **bone sclerosis** (hardening or thickening of the bone). The absence of sclerosis is key; MM typically destroys bone without the body reacting by building new dense bone around the edges.
*   **Metastatic Carcinoma (LMC):** Characterized by **relatively large and restricted defects**. In the Kitami skeleton, Suzuki noted that in the parietal region (the side of the skull), there were "numerous concentrated small lytic defects" that, when viewed together, formed a "comparatively large osteolytic lesion." On X-rays, this appeared as an "obscure and relatively large osteolytic shadow." This clustering of smaller defects into a larger mass is a hallmark of metastatic spread, distinguishing it from the uniform, scattered holes of MM.

For Ghalioungui, $^{11}$ the differentiation distinction 'of bones showing a destructive process with metastatic osteolytic lesions . . . from MM . . . may be impossible'. At the same time, according to him, it would be erroneous to use in the diagnosis modern statistical data on the incidence of both disorders.

To understand the significance of these findings, it is helpful to visualize the structure of the skull. The skull is not a single solid block of bone; rather, it is often composed of two dense outer plates (the outer and inner tables) separated by a spongy, honeycomb-like middle layer called the **diploic layer** (in the cranium) or the **spongiotic layer** (in the jaw). Think of this middle layer as the "soft center" of a sandwich, while the outer tables are the crust. When we see lesions described as "punched-out" and confined to these spongy layers, it suggests that the disease process is targeting the marrow space within the bone rather than destroying the structural integrity of the outer shell immediately. The absence of "reaction" around these foci is a critical diagnostic clue. In many bone diseases, the body attempts to wall off the infection or tumor, creating a rim of new, dense bone (sclerosis). The lack of this reactive rim here indicates a process that is either too aggressive for the body to respond to, or one that suppresses the normal healing response.
Both cases from Abusir were more characteristic of MM than of LMC, but the latter could not be rejected fully, especially in the second case. The male sex would favour a diagnosis of MM.

Here, the text introduces two competing diagnoses: **MM** (Multiple Myeloma) and **LMC** (Leukemic Metastatic Carcinoma, or more broadly, metastatic carcinoma). This distinction is vital because it changes our understanding of the disease's origin. Multiple Myeloma is a primary cancer of the plasma cells (a type of white blood cell) found in the bone marrow. It is a disease that starts *in* the bone. In contrast, LMC refers to cancer that has spread *to* the bone from a primary tumor elsewhere in the body (such as the breast, lung, or prostate).

Why does the text state that "male sex would favour a diagnosis of MM"? This is a statistical observation based on epidemiology. While both men and women can develop these conditions, the demographic profiles differ slightly. However, the more critical differentiator often lies in the morphology of the lesions and the patient's age, which we will see in the next case. The fact that LMC "could not be rejected fully" highlights the difficulty in paleopathology: without modern tissue samples or blood tests, we must rely on the visual "signature" of the bone destruction. A "punched-out" lesion is a classic hallmark of Multiple Myeloma, but metastatic cancers can sometimes mimic this appearance, leading to diagnostic uncertainty.

The first skull from Saqqara, from a 40-60-year-old female, revealed under macroscopic investigation several defects in the skull vault, right orbit and body of the occipital bone. Their size was slightly more variable, ranging from 4 to 13 mm in diameter. Their outline was, however, irregular. Some were surrounded by zones of minute pores, and the defect grew through the clustering and merging of these pores. In the radiographs, a few lucid foci could be found in the cranial vault and right orbit. They were not sharply delimited, but had a cloudy appearance (Figure 3).

Let us pause to examine the terminology used here, as it provides a window into the biological process. The term **"lucid foci"** refers to areas that appear lighter or darker (depending on the X-ray orientation) on the radiograph because they are less dense than the surrounding healthy bone. In simple terms, these are "holes" or areas where bone has been lost.

The description of the outline as **"irregular"** and the presence of **"zones of minute pores"** is a crucial diagnostic feature. Unlike the "punched-out" lesions of the Abusir cases, which had clean, sharp edges, these lesions look messy. The text explains that the defect grew through the "clustering and merging of these pores." Imagine a sponge. If you slowly dissolve the material in one spot, the holes don't appear as a single clean circle; instead, the tiny existing air pockets in the sponge expand and merge, creating an irregular, jagged void. This "cloudy" or "ill-defined" appearance on the X-ray, rather than a sharp black circle, suggests a different pathological mechanism. It implies that the bone destruction is occurring within the trabecular (spongy) bone in a way that blurs the boundaries, rather than cleanly cutting through it. This "cloudy" look is often associated with metastatic disease (LMC) where the tumor infiltrates the bone marrow and disrupts the normal bone architecture in a more diffuse, less organized manner than the discrete plasma cell tumors of Multiple Myeloma.

The second skull from Saqqara, from a 30–40-year-old female, did not show any macroscopic defect. It was X-rayed only because of an osteoma of the left parietal bone. The radiographs revealed a number of lucid foci of
roundish shape irregularly scattered in the diploic layer of the vault from miniscule to 7 mm diam. These were also cloudy in appearance.

This case presents a fascinating challenge for the investigator. Macroscopically, meaning with the naked eye, the skull looked normal. There were no visible holes or defects. The X-ray was performed incidentally, because the researcher was already looking at the skull for an **osteoma**—a benign, slow-growing bone tumor that is common and usually harmless. It is a bit like finding a hidden cavity in a tooth only after getting an X-ray for a routine checkup.

However, the X-ray revealed the truth: a "number of lucid foci" scattered in the diploic layer. The fact that these were "miniscule" and "cloudy" reinforces the pattern seen in the first Saqqara case. The lesions were too small to break through the outer table of the bone to be seen by eye, but they were clearly present in the spongy interior. This highlights the power of radiography in paleopathology: it allows us to see the "hidden" pathology that the surface of the bone conceals. The "roundish shape" here is slightly different from the "irregular" description of the first case, but the "cloudy" appearance remains the key unifying feature, pointing away from the sharp, clean edges of classic Multiple Myeloma.

Both cases from Saqqara were more characteristic of LMC than of MM, but also here, especially in the second case, the possibility of MM had to be taken into account. The female sex would favour a carcinoma with a probable primary location in the breast.

Here, the expert makes a probabilistic judgment. The "cloudy," irregular, and porous nature of the lesions in these two female individuals aligns more closely with the known radiological signatures of metastatic carcinoma (LMC) than with Multiple Myeloma. Why does the text suggest a "probable primary location in the breast"? This is a logical deduction based on epidemiology and metastatic patterns. Breast cancer is one of the most common cancers in women, and it has a well-documented propensity to metastasize to the bones, particularly the skull and spine. In a historical context where we cannot perform a biopsy, the combination of female sex, age, and the specific "cloudy" bone destruction pattern makes breast cancer the most statistically likely primary source. However, the caution "the possibility of MM had to be taken into account" remains. This is a reminder that in medicine and paleopathology, we rarely deal in absolute certainties; we deal in probabilities. The "cloudy" appearance is a strong indicator, but not an absolute proof, and the differential diagnosis must always remain open until all evidence is weighed.

A more persuasive case of LMC was detected recently in a 35-45-year-old female from the Christian cemetery K at Sayala, Egyptian Nubia, dated to sixth to eleventh century AD. $^{18,19}$ Four defects were apparent in the skull macroscopically. The largest one 16mm diam. had a complete perforation in the right upper frontal region; another, less advanced, defect was towards the surface in the left upper frontal region (a pigmented zone of 25 mm diam. with two small fissures); a small perforation lay on the left parietal (1 mm diam.) and a large area of destruction was present in the left half of occipital base (24 mm diam.) penetrating deeply into its spongiotic layer. The first three lesions, together with a few tiny ones in the rear third of the skull, which did not perforate the outer table, can be found in the lateral radiograph (Figure 4). About 40 similar lesions (1-25 mm diam.) were detected macroscopically and about 20-30 additional lesions were detected radio-

graphically in the vertebrae, sacrum, ribs, manubrium sterni, scapulae, left clavicle and radius, a few proximal hand phalanges and a single metacarpal, in both ossa coxae and the left femur and tibia. Histological sections prepared by M. Schultz revealed Howship's lacunae, typical for osteoclastic erosion. The character of the defects was predominantly lytic with a slight sclerotic reaction and bone remodelling. They apparently started as tiny openings, which merged and resulted in larger perforations. Their edges were uneven, crenulated or frayed, and surrounded by areas of minute pores. On radiographs they appeared soft, with obscure edges.
Many features are common to both MM

Their incidence is multiple and polytopic, their character is exclusively or predominantly lytic, they originate in the marrow of the cancellous bone, and they progress through erosion of the inner side of the compact bone, undermining, and sometimes slightly lifting, the edge. The range of affected bone is: the vertebrae and sacrum, the ribs and sternum, the pelvis, the skull, and the proximal ends of both the femur and humerus. The lesions occur only rarely distal to the elbow and knee. Pathological fractures — compressions of the vertebrae, multiple transverse breaks of the ribs or long bone fracture — may occur in more advanced cases. Both malignancies have a predilection for individuals of 40 or older.
Combining the experience of various authors with our own, we would like to point out differentiating features.
(i) The density of the lesions is great in MM, whose foci are very numerous and scattered through the skeleton while in LMC the lesions are less numerous and more localized.
(ii) The form of the outline of the lesions is regularly round (circular to slightly oval) in MM, while they are more irregular with denticulations and scallops in LMC.

(iii) The size of the lesions is more consistent, small to medium (up to several milimetres) in
MM, with the exception of foci that merge together. In LMC, their size is more variable, small to large (up to several centimetres).
(iv) Observed macroscopically, the edges of the lesions are sharp and appear as punched-out or bored in MM, while they are scalloped, denticulated or craggy in LMC.
(v) In radiographs, the observed areas of lucidity are clearly and sharply delimited in MM, while they appear obscure, cloudy or 'moth-eaten' in LMC.

(vi) The surface of the surrounding bone is smooth without any pathological change in MM, while it might be pitted with further tiny apertures in LMC, which constitute a zone of potential enlargement of the central lytic lesion through gradual merging.

(vii) The occurrence of an osteoblastic reaction, observable macroscopically at the edges of the lesions or in the trabeculae of the denuded spongiotic bone, as well as radiographically as a zone of increased density around the lesion, is non-existent or extremely slight in quickly progressing MM, while it may be slight or significant in LMC. (viii) A certain topographic predilection was observed by a few investigators. Scapula (glenoid fossa, axillary border and acromion), clavicle (lateral portion), radius and ulna are more typical sites for MM, while the neural arches of the vertebrae and their various processes seems to be more frequently affected in LMC.

(ix) Sexual predilection, deduced from recent statistics, may be applied as well: in MM, males are afflicted twice as often as females, while LMC can be expected to occur more commonly in females, owing especially to longer lasting breast cancer, which did not threaten life in past populations as much as cancers of the important inner organs.

The recent rarity of MM and the common incidence of LMC, quoted by some of the authors, should not be taken as a differential diagnostic criterion because the situation in the past could have been completely different.

In conclusion we must stress that the most important condition for a successful distinction between MM and LMC in dry bone is the

preservation of a whole skeleton. Even then, as is true in other branches of biology, a few borderline cases will remain whose diagnosis will be ambiguous. In screening ancient materials for malignancies the use of radiography is to be highly recommended.
